item.title: [YC Root Access] Centralize is the GPS for Enterprise Deals
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：Centralize 卖的不是"数据"，而是"组织的失忆症解药"

大多数销售工具在解决"我不认识谁"的问题，但 Centralize 真正解决的是一个更隐蔽、也更昂贵的问题——企业级组织的集体失忆。视频里那个 Fortune 10 案例的关键细节被轻描淡写地一带而过：那位销售赢单的关键，不是他自己两年前的对话，而是他团队里某个人两年前的对话，而他当时根本不在场。

这里藏着一个惊人的事实：在大型企业销售里，公司知道的东西，永远远多于任何一个员工知道的东西，但这些知识从未被"提取"出来。CRM 之所以失败了二十年，是因为它假设人会主动写下自己知道的东西；Centralize 反其道而行之——它假设人什么都不会主动记录，然后从邮件、会议、Slack、LinkedIn 里"考古"出组织本来就拥有、但从未意识到自己拥有的关系资本。

这本质上是一场"隐形资产的资产负债表化"运动。 每家公司都有一张看不见的关系资产负债表，Centralize 把它变成了可查询的、可视化的、可交易的资产。

跨领域连接：这其实是"分子生物学"的销售版本

有趣的是，Centralize 内部称之为 "trust graph"（信任图谱），而它的核心技术挑战——entity resolution（实体消解）——正是蛋白质组学和药物发现里最难的问题：如何在噪声巨大的多源数据里，判断"这两个信号指的是同一个分子"。

生物学家用质谱、抗体、序列比对来做这件事；Centralize 用邮件签名、职位变动、社交痕迹来做同样的事。两者的深层同构在于：它们都在把"离散的观察"缝合成"持续的实体轨迹"。而一旦你能追踪单个实体的完整轨迹，你就从"描述性科学"跃升到了"预测性科学"——生物学里预测的是药物作用，销售里预测的则是"谁能在下周把这个 deal 推进一步"。

更进一步的类比是流行病学里的接触追踪：Centralize 做的事情几乎是"信任的接触追踪"——不是追踪病毒如何在人群里传播，而是追踪"影响力和推荐"如何在职场网络里传播。这个类比揭示了它未来最大的护城河可能不是数据，而是图的时间演化（人跳槽后关系如何衰减？信任如何随时间迁移到新公司？）。

打破常规的预测：Centralize 最大的敌人可能是它自己的成功

一个隐藏的系统性张力：当所有卖家都用 Centralize 时，"关系"作为差异化优势会开始贬值。这就是金融市场里的"阿尔法衰减"——任何被广泛使用的信号最终都会失去预测力。

但这里有一个反转，也是我认为团队可能还没完全意识到的深层机会：Centralize 不会退化为"关系版 ZoomInfo"，它会演化为"企业内部的社会资本交易所"。想想看——一旦每个 champion 都能看到"自己是被谁选中作为通往 CEO 的路径"，一旦每个高管都能看到"自己被多少家供应商标记为关键节点"，那么关系本身就从模糊的社交资本变成了可被定价、被交换、被博弈的显性资源。

这带来一个哲学层面的意外后果：Centralize 声称在"帮助 champion"，但从系统层面看，它其实在加速企业内部权力结构的透明化。这和维基解密之于政府、Glassdoor 之于雇主是同一类现象——当隐性权力被强制可视化，权力本身的运作逻辑会被迫改变。

那句 "you don't win alone. You have to win with your champion" 听起来是句销售格言，但它其实在描述一种正在发生的组织学变革：未来的企业销售，不再是"公司 vs 公司"，而是"跨公司的临时联盟 vs 跨公司的临时联盟"。Centralize 恰好在这个变革的最上游卡了位。

📝 转录文本

开场：介绍与融资

主持人： I'm excited today to welcome the founders of Centralize. Here's Ratchet and Will. So, you guys just closed a $15 million series A led by NEA. Tell us — what does Centralize do?

Ratchet： Yeah, well, first off, thanks for having us here. It's a — it's a very cool full circle moment being back.

Centralized is the GPS for your enterprise deals. In short, it's automatic org charts that create themselves, and they effectively show you who you know, the people who's missing, and then how do you fill in the white space. So, kind of the turn-by-turn directions of the relationships that really define whether or not you lose or win these top accounts.

早期客户

主持人： And who are some of the top customers that are live with you?

Ratchet： Yeah, privileged to have some pretty awesome folks in the last few months. So we got the teams over at Decagon, Langchain, Cognition, uh Intercom, Brex, Exa — list goes on, but a lot of really great folks.

核心原语：客户的客户的 Org Chart

主持人： I think you guys told me about one primitive that you guys figured out was basically you guys are shipping the org chart of your customers' customers. Tell me about all the inputs you take in and how you build this — and maybe a case study on how building an org chart for your customer's customers brings value.

Will： We call it the trust graph internally, and — well, you could probably talk about the inputs.

I mean, I think — uh, it's actually really fascinating, I think, to what Ratchet and I were talking about a little bit earlier. There's a lot of different inputs, right? There's a lot of unstructured data, whether that's emails, whether that's calls, all the places that you might be talking to the prospect, to the customer in. We kind of just suck all of that in and then understand all of the human dynamics between all of that information.

And so when we do that, we take all of that and then we almost just like parse it into a visual that anyone looking at this account or anyone looking at the customer can really quickly see and get the context for: what are the relationships, where are they, where do people live on the organization — and then immediately what's empty. Like, "oh, we don't have anyone at the VP level. What do we do? Who do we go after?" And centralized kind of uses AI to help you understand that.

底层技术：实体消解

And so a lot of it is — Ratchet mentioned this a little bit earlier — but entity resolution. So, hey, is this the same Ratchet that uh was at Meta a while back, that was at A to B a while back? That's the same Ratchet that's now at Centralized. How does Centralized go and figure that out under the hood? And a lot of that ends up just being a bunch of fun engineering um to make that happen.

And so the underlying — I think interesting part of centralized is the way that we've structured the actual product, the actual data model, to actually be really focused on the person, the messy middle of the dynamics between two people. If I had a conversation now, how does our conversation today change over time? Like, if we have a conversation tomorrow, what changes about our relationship? That's what centralized captures — at an organization level.

主持人： So if — if I'm trying to sell to you guys, to Centralize, it would map up all the stakeholders taking all — from what I understand — calls, emails, Serums, Word tickets, my LinkedIn connections, and build this uh traversal graph.

Ratchet： Yes.

案例研究：Fortune 10 客户与八位数合同

主持人： Tell us a bit about um the outcomes of uh some of the customers that use you, and what do they get from using you now that you have this custom org chart per customer?

Ratchet： Yeah, it's really cool. I mean, we have again customers like Langchain, Cognition — like the AI natives that won't build it or can't build it. And I think a lot of it is, is to's point, because that entity resolution layer is such a core and uh almost like underlying that we can build and provide.

一场 Fortune 10 的赢单故事

So to answer your question directly — how's this already accelerating today? Well, we have a lot of these customers, enterprise strat teams using centralized, and there's an example where one of them um — of the names I listed — was working a Fortune 10. And these are like insane accounts, right? Thousands of people. How could you hope to navigate this like crazy sea, let alone you do it once, and then normally you know someone leaves tomorrow, a new conversation happen you weren't a part of — it's just changing underneath you.

But they were able to wake up, for that Fortune 10, to not only the relationship trust graph of who we've ever talked to — and importantly, not just that that rep had talked to, but his team had talked to two years ago. He wasn't even in the room for it, but — picture that — institutional memory is now finally visualized.

Right? You wake up that whole story: who his board is connected to that used to work somewhere at DBT, whose friend is now at the prospect, and all of a sudden you have a friendly internally to walk you into that deal. You're breaking through that trust — kind of the the the gap that you have to bridge.

And then finally, the names that match their ICP of the personas they normally have to get to, that would normally take hours if not weeks of trolling through — hopefully it's in LinkedIn or your friend groups, like wherever you have to go to find those answers — Centralized has given you the players on the field, warm or cold, already pre-mapped out.

Champion 视角：把地图交给盟友

And I think the coolest use case is — as much as this is an internal dual strategy board, it's like the chess board you're playing with — any good seller, probably most people listening here know, you don't win alone. You have to win with your champion. You have someone that's helping you because they want you to win, they want the product.

How do you help them internally? What if you show them the map for the first time, that they can see with not just who you have, but who you think we need to get to, and literally help them become a champion.

In this case, on the call, they literally went from a six-month sales cycle that was taking them literally half a year to try to make progress — and they were stuck — to a warm pathway that their head of marketing had into the C-suite, and got walked in showing their champion the map of that relationship and being given the missing org they didn't even know that existed, because their champion could finally see it. And ultimately progressing and closing the deal for an eight-figure outcome.

主持人： Eight figures. So they closed a eight-figure contract in a matter of months. This is —

Ratchet： And that was, by the way, six months into the cycle pre-Centralized, and post-Centralized it took them on the order of weeks to get those outcomes. So imagine if they just started every deal using Centralized.

目标用户与 Single Player Mode

主持人： So who should use you?

Ratchet： I think first and foremost, it's folks that are on the ground, right — the people that are actually moving the needle working these deals. Typically — I mean, all of our customers — it's the enterprise and strategic AEs and SDRs for the front of the house, to W's point, navigating multi-threading, breaking into the deal.

And then very naturally after — haven't forgotten about our friends on the CS side and post-sales — it's still how do you retain that account? Do you have the right people that close that are still around? Have they left underneath you? Have they shifted? Or the AMs, account managers that are expanding those accounts too? It's really the entire revenue org.

So, if anyone is navigating complex stakeholder deals and has to understand people, and that's critical to winning or losing the deal, it's a no-brainer to use Centralized.

Single Player Mode 发布

Maybe the fun thing that actually will make this even easier for everyone is — not only did we announce the Series A last Wednesday, but last Thursday we announced Single Player Mode. In short, Centralized is free for any individual to try out for the first time. So, literally have at it, right? Like everyone should be able to leverage uh this new way of selling and building relationships.

招聘：寻找高 Agency 的建造者

主持人： So you guys are growing very quickly. Who are the type of people that really succeed at Centralize?

Will： The one word that all of us boils down to, I think, no matter the role that we're looking for, is agency. So, anyone that has high ownership, um, that is able to run through walls to get things done, uh is going to do really well at Centralized, and are people that do really well in our interview process as well.

I think Fresh and I, you know, we're building this company right now as we go. We're looking for fellow builders that can come in with really really high agency um to do that with us.

I think right now we're looking for engineers and go-to-market folks. Um, really anyone — uh full stack, high agency, AI engineers, go-to-market across the stack. I really think if you're any one of those people and you're cracked, please come talk to us. Um and yeah, if you have high agency, I would love to talk to you.

结束语

主持人： All right, congratulations so much, and thank you so much for coming, guys.

Ratchet / Will： Thanks for having us. This is great.

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Is Robinhood's Tokenized AMC Stock Actually Illegal?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"反向 ADR"革命：这不是衍生品之争，而是资本主权之争

大多数人把 AMC vs Robinhood 之争看作"合规打架"，但真正被埋没的洞察是：Robinhood 做的是一个"反向 ADR"（Reverse ADR） —— 传统 ADR 是把外国股票包装进美国市场，而 Robinhood 是把美国股票包装出美国、送到全球。这个方向的翻转其实是二战后美元霸权逻辑在链上的镜像延续。

一个让人意外的观察：AMC CEO 骂 Robinhood 骂得越凶，AMC 股价越涨（一夜 21%）。这不是巧合，而是揭示了一个新的市场微观结构规律 —— 在 attention 经济里，被 tokenize 本身就是一种"上市二次 IPO"。链上的 mimetic demand 会反哺链下股价。这与传统金融理论完全相反：传统认为衍生品是从标的派生价值，而在 meme + token 时代，衍生层反过来给标的注入了"社交流动性溢价"。Adam Aron 在骂人的同时，其实在给自己的股票做全球免费营销。

二、跨领域连接：AI 数据中心的政治困局 = 19 世纪铁路+新教伦理的镜像

Chris 提到"数据中心可能成为中期选举的核心议题"，这个观察被大部分人低估了。但真正有趣的类比是：当前 AI Lab 的处境，几乎完美复刻了 19 世纪美国铁路大亨的历史节点。

  • 铁路巨头当年也说"我们要重塑美国"→ 引发平民主义反弹（Populist Movement, 1892）
  • Sam Altman 说"我们要拿走所有工作"→ Bernie Sanders 提议禁止超级智能
  • 铁路 tycoons 也曾被指责"用蒸汽机替代人类"
  • 反对铁路的核心不是技术，而是"谁掌握了未来的定义权"

Austin 说的那句"AI Lab 应该走出硅谷去俄克拉荷马"其实指向一个更深的结构性问题：这一轮 AI 建设是历史上第一次"资本极度密集但劳动力零参与"的基础设施建设。铁路至少雇佣了华工和爱尔兰劳工，电网建设创造了国家电工阶级，互联网创造了程序员中产。而数据中心，只有噪声、耗电、税收，没有一个"我们家孩子在里面上班"的社会锚点。这就是为什么两党会罕见地对齐 —— 政治学家把这称为"无从属性基础设施悖论"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：三个战场其实是同一个战场

如果你把 AMC/Robinhood、AI 监管、Fed 加息、挪威主权基金减持美债 这四件事分开看，它们是四条新闻。但如果把它们叠加，会浮现一个统一的元结构：

在美国国内合法性衰减的临界点上，一切"边缘、离岸、链上"的替代路径都在同时被激活。

  • Robinhood 把股票送去 Jersey（境外）→ 因为美国监管让 capital formation 变贵
  • 全球用户通过 VPN 买美国资产 → 因为本国监管让财富保全变难
  • Norway 减持美债 → 因为美国政治干预 Fed 让主权风险变大
  • Bernie 提议禁 AI → 因为技术精英对普通人的"存在性焦虑"提供的答案不合格

Ram 说"要拥有能在名义价格上重定价的资产"，这个建议表面是宏观策略，本质上是在说：当制度信用被稀释，物理稀缺性和现金流稀缺性就成了唯一的锚。而这也解释了为什么 meme coin 和数据中心概念股在同一时期同时爆发 —— 它们分别代表了注意力的稀缺性和电力/算力的稀缺性，是同一个通胀防御逻辑的两个极端。

啊哈时刻：Cheesecake Factory 今年跑赢大多数半导体股 —— Austin 一句玩笑话里藏着这一集最深的信号：当高端叙事集体高估，"能被吃、能被摸、能被使用"的真实业务反而在悄悄地重新赢回估值权。这是一个静默的"物质主义反扑"。

📝 转录文本

开场：三条宏观论断

We're not going to see rate hikes. Kevin Warsh is talking like a hawk, but he's a dove.

Two, we got productivity growth bailout coming from AI. That's going to save the day. We are in this disinflationary period with these temporary price shocks due to geopolitical concerns, energy production's a bit higher than ever, and it's going to continue to go up.

Three, the AI buildout itself is inflationary. It's contributing like a point and a half the GDP. So that is part of the cost of this buildout. They're not going to get down to the 2% inflation target for at least a few years. That means that you should be owning assets that reprice in nominal terms, especially equities that are indexed to the data center theme.

欢迎与广告

Hey everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. Today is Monday, September 7th, Labor Day here in the United States, and we're still here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro.

So before we begin, a quick commercial break. This episode is brought to you by 1inch Aqua, the shared liquidity layer from 1inch. Back multiple liquidity positions with one wallet balance and keep your tokens in your wallet until a swap fills. See how it works at oneinch.com/Aqua.

All right, everybody, as always, I'm your host, Austin Campbell, high scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I'm here with Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto.

一、AMC vs Robinhood：Tokenized 股票之争

事件背景

And Chris, today we're going to start with a fight. So over the weekend, AMC CEO Adam Aaron went after Robinhood's tokenized AMC shares issued out of Jersey by Robinhood Assets, calling them, quote, "contemptible, outrageous, disgusting, detestable, inexcusable, vile."

He said AMC has no connection to it and does not condone it. Vlad Tenev's entire reply was, "What's the concern?" And Aaron's answer was eight paragraphs and a demand that Robinhood voluntarily cease and — kiss, it was misspelled — desist, with Robinhood CLO Dan Gallagher, notably former SEC, saying, "Send your lawyers and we'll educate them."

Tenev, in the same minute, said, "We stand behind stock tokens." Now, weirdly, AMC stock jumped nearly 21% overnight to $3.07 on this fight, according to The Block.

什么是 Stock Token？

And I think where to start is, what is a stock token? So in this case, tokenized debt securities issued by Robinhood Assets expose people to the share price — not the ownership, not the shareholder rights. They are unregistered in the U.S. They are not offered to U.S. persons.

So the substantive charge that synthetic equity decouples stock token ownership and a company having an ability to control its own capital raising efforts, and that it sows distrust in markets generally. But the flip side is there's 13.4 billion of these things.

And to have some sort of price token like this, you're either creating a derivative, which Robinhood did not really do here, or having the reverse of what is called an ADR. That is to say, you have stocks that are backing this token, which you pass the price reference on for.

So previously, OpenAI had disavowed Robinhood's tokens in July 2025. But this to me is a little bit different. OpenAI is not a public company. These are not publicly tradable. That is private stock. Often you need issuer permission for transfers in private stock in a way you do not with public stock. So while this fight has happened once before, it was not the exact same fight.

Chris 的评论：创新与资本形成的冲突

Chris, you have a lot of thoughts on tokenization. You have been involved in this space for a while. What do you make of this dispute between AMC and Robinhood?

Chris: I mean, there's so much going on right now where you're seeing innovation, creativity. I'm sure we're going to talk about some of the meme coin stuff pairings that are also going on Robinhood chain, which are very hard to discuss at work because of the names involved. But gosh, I haven't seen this type of innovation and creativity for decades, post-global financial crisis.

I totally understand the challenges, but like, you know, you were at Wall Street. I was on Wall Street. Synthetic products are a thing — they're everywhere. And I think the challenge here, did Robinhood do anything illegal? I think it's very clear that they've done their homework if you listen to their general counsel.

The second question is, okay, why is there conflict here? Well, if you're a CEO, you would love for someone to buy your equity rather than... because capital markets — U.S. capital markets are where they are today because it's a place for capital formation if you're a company. And so they're making the principles argument saying, wait a second, this isn't right. This isn't fair because you're undermining the principles of capital formation. And frankly, that's one of the core goals of the SEC to ensure that capital formation is available and thoughtfully takes place here in the United States.

And so that's the conflict. It's like, hey, you're messing with my capital formation. But again, you go to a Delta One desk on Wall Street, there's constantly structures, there's constantly synthetic capabilities.

I'm a little bit surprised that there isn't more coordination. I would think in the future you're going to see companies — like right now it's conflictual, right, where AMC and Robinhood are fighting with each other. I think the next iteration of this are real companies working closely with these mass distributors and really finding ways to distribute true tokenized equities for capital formation. Right now, everyone's like every man for himself, but I think in the future, you're going to see more partnerships being formed, and that's where the real value is going to take place.

Ram 加入：衍生品需要真实用例

Ram: Happy Labor Day. In our family, we call it Happy Capitalism Day. Let's go innovation, let's go American enterprise, let's go productivity growth, technology.

A few things. One, capital formation is critical. Derivatives don't create capital formation — it's risk transfer. Derivatives play an incredibly important role. Like you go back to the original use case of the farmer planning for the harvest — they've got uncertainty on the price when they deliver to the market versus all the cost, time, labor they put into it. And derivatives played a very important role in that risk transfer. That's win-win for everybody. That helps Coca-Cola, helps McDonald's manage cattle prices, sugar inputs, helps the end consumer manage inflation. Same story is true for oil.

And I think the AI labs are making a mistake, spending all of their time in a circle jerk in Silicon Valley, like talking about AI safety, instead of just being out there trying to cure as much cancer as humanly possible and then demonstrate that loudly to people.

So my number one advice to these people, if you want to stop the data center backlash, is get out of Silicon Valley. Go to places like Idaho. Go to Texas. Go to Oklahoma City. Go to Nebraska. Go to North Carolina. Go meet actual people. Go to those communities. Find out what's important. Find out what they care about, and then demonstrate value for them. Because otherwise, they're rightly going to be pissed, right, that you're essentially just ignoring them. And it's incredible for people who are allegedly so smart to be so incredibly tone-deaf about politics. Get ready to talk about data centers during Thanksgiving. Oh my god.

四、Warsh、加息与利率之争

Warsh 与 Waller 表态

All right, well, let's close here on one other thing that people will definitely unfortunately be talking about at Thanksgiving, which is Warsh and hikes.

So Chair Kevin Warsh put September on the table at Jackson Hole on August 28th, saying the Fed has work to do on inflation. Traders now think there's a 58% chance of a hike in September. Hilariously, Warsh, understanding a little bit about how algorithms work, also used the word "hike," literally meaning going for a hike, repeatedly at the start of his speech, knowing what it would do to algos. I just want to say as a former volatility trader, next time, buddy, get "hike" and "cut" in there at least three times each, and you're really going to cause things to go crazy.

But that aside, Waller came out on Thursday and said he'd support a hold if disinflation holds up. But if it, quote, "if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike." He judges policy currently only slightly restricting aggregate demand. Waller was talking about core being 3.3% and three-month core has come down. But again, future data seems to be what's driving this.

Crypto took this as a dovish read. Bitcoin ran up. Spot Bitcoin ETFs continue to take money in. And then Friday showed up and payrolls came in at plus 162k against a 56k consensus. And interestingly, July was revised up to plus 21k from a previous decline of 23k. This is reversing a trend where payrolls have consistently been revised down over and over for a while here.

政治覆盖层与美联储

So essentially what we're looking at here is the political overlay is becoming real. Trump is saying, "Lower the rate or I'll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit," calling this an embargo better than tariffs, and telling the Fed board to, quote, "be patriots for a change." But on the other hand, we have all these people at the Fed essentially expressing caution.

So Ram, I want to start with you. I know you've been watching rates markets as a driver for equities here. What are you taking from the chaos around this whole debate?

Ram: We're not going to see rate hikes. Kevin Warsh is talking like a hawk but he's a dove. Two, we got productivity growth bailout coming from AI. That's going to save the day. We are in this disinflationary period with these temporary price shocks due to geopolitical concerns. Energy productions are a bit higher than ever, and it's going to continue to go up. Three, the AI buildout itself is inflationary. It's contributing like a point and a half of the GDP. So that is part of the cost of this buildout. They're not going to get down to the 2% inflation target for at least a few years. That means that you should be owning assets that reprice in nominal terms, especially equities that are indexed to the data center theme.

Chris：柴油价格与中期选举

Austin: Chris, what do you think? Are we getting a hike in September?

Chris: I agree with Rob, speaking for myself, but a couple of things that I'm watching is diesel. Diesel is hitting record shattering prices, I think averaging like $5.85 a gallon. That hits real America, that hits the truck drivers. And so it's no surprise, off goes Kushner and Wyckoff to Russia and Ukraine, because a lot of that's hurting supply.

And so if you're Trump right now, your eyes on midterm elections, you don't want to go through impeachment after impeachment if the Congress turns. So you need to keep as many seats as possible. How do you do that? You got to attack inflation. There are some things hopefully he can do to help control that vis-a-vis the Middle East. He's been trying to do that. It's been difficult. Bessent needs rates down, which is another challenge.

And so to me, I don't think anyone's in a position to raise rates under this environment, whether they're independent or not, we can decide. But what can he do to bring inflation down? Is there anything within his control? Because he has to perform well in midterms. Inflation will hurt midterms. And people are watching markets as well. So it's all about that from my perspective, and he's going to try to do whatever it takes.

Austin：口炮 Fed 反而推高长端利率

Austin: One of the interesting things to me about Trump is I feel like he's very much clearly a real estate and equities guy with the way he talks about markets. Because jawboning the Fed as the president will cause rates to go up. Let me say that as a former rates trader. Because people will look at this and say, "Ah, what is going to happen on a long enough timeline is the central bank will be captured by political interests, which means I should trust this country less, which means that I should demand more for the bonds."

To be clear, every time Trump shit talks the Fed, add a basis point to the 30-year, kind of what's going on in my head, right? Like he's actually moving rates up with this behavior, not down. So the constant political threats seem not to work the way he thinks in rates markets.

The other part of it is, Chris, you were just alluding to this, and I think you're correct. If this is a supply shock, there's not much the Fed is going to be able to do to address this thing just by moving rates around, because the level of interest rates does not create atoms, right? What we need is more fuel physically to do this.

Now, is there some level where the Fed could get rates high enough that we've destroyed demand? Yes. Is anybody going to enjoy that outcome when we cause a massive recession as Volcker did in the early 80s? Absolutely not.

国会才是问题所在

And so I look at all of this and I see Bessent talking about it. I see the Fed talking about it. I see Trump talking about it. And the great irony is over here who needs to talk about it and is not talking about it is Congress. Because fundamentally, I think all of these three guys are like pushing on a string until Congress stops spending so much money. Do you think I'm wrong about that? What do you think?

Chris: Yeah, where I am — you're totally wrong. There's no way Congress is going to stop spending money. Like how is that a viable outcome? Seriously?

Austin: I mean, okay, one, I think in the current framework they're not, but I would tell people in general you should probably expect inflation to continue if Congress is not going to stop spending money, right? Like the balance of payments thing is real, and eventually the pain will become severe enough that they're going to have to change their behavior. But Chris, you're right, it's usually got to get a lot worse than where we are now before people start actually reacting to it. Maybe we should wait till after midterms.

I mean, in fairness to the poor guy, Paul Ryan started talking about this what, close to 10 years ago, and they immediately kicked him out of Congress. So I guess there's precedent for not doing that.

Rom, what do you think? Do you think I'm wrong on just like it's a raw balance of payments issue in the end?

Ram: Inflation will be sticky for a while. I think for all the reasons that we've talked about. So the main thing you should just do is position your portfolio accordingly. Own real assets that have earnings growth, where you're a beneficiary of inflation.

挪威主权财富基金减持美债

Austin: I don't think that's wrong. And to that end, we're starting to see other people reacting in this way in the market. Like Norway is a good example. So Norway, I think it's the world's largest sovereign wealth fund at $2.3 trillion — certainly the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, if not — it's close if it's not the largest — recommended that the government bond share for U.S. bonds fall from 70% to 50% with treasuries taking the largest cut. So that's $80 billion off $215 billion of treasuries held at the end of June, and the slice going from 34.1 to 21.9%.

So you're starting to see people who are professional money managers, long-term focus, not captured by U.S. local interests, starting to bail out on U.S. debt, especially long-dated U.S. debt. Like, do you guys think that's signal or do you think something else is going on here?

Ram: No, those are headlines you see when rates are topping out. That's it. I'm waiting for the viral Ray Dalio Economic Machine thing to go out. That'll be the top. That's when you go — that'll be the time you actually buy bonds. You want that. That's when you buy the bonds. Yeah, this is just what you expect to see during moments like this.

1994 类比与利率顶部

Austin: Yeah, I mean, so where I'm finding it harder to interpret this than usual is, Ram, my gut is to agree with you. You look at these things and you say to people, well, when people complain like this and when all the usual talking heads are on and when you're getting front page articles about this — like when the Time cover saying U.S. Treasuries are dead comes out, you buy Treasuries, right? Like classic signal.

The flip side though, and Chris, we've seen this in Asia in the 90s — sometimes when you lose hold of the rope, it can go a lot further than you thought before you get your hands back on it. Yeah, I agree. We saw — god, I can't remember what it was, I'm seeing if I can look it up — that there was, yeah, it's HSBC, noting parallels to 1997. So this was Frederick Newman — surging U.S. yields, weak yen, unbridled tech optimism. And there the ten-year climbed from 5% in '93 to nearly 8% by October 1994.

Now obviously, had you bought it at 8%, you made a killing. But, Ram, I guess I'll ask you, are you saying you think the top is near here in rates terms, or are you just saying watch for the signals and maybe it's got room to run?

Ram: Yeah, no, I think you're in the 8th or 9th inning around rates. There's an outside shot that runs to 5%, but if that happens, that's the top. You should be a better buyer of rate-sensitive securities. I see in the equity market too, it's not just the bond market. You have all sorts of rate-sensitive stocks that are cheap. Like solar names, surprisingly, are rate-sensitive. Building supply material names and homebuilders are rate-sensitive. These companies have lots of debt. So I think you should be looking at opportunities in those areas.

保险板块的角度

Chris: How are you feeling about the insurance sector, if this is your view on rates?

Ram: That's a really good question. Because as you know, insurance companies are balance sheets that are publicly traded. They've taken premiums and deployed, and they go buy bonds and equities and longer-duration assets. So when rates go up, the fair value of their balance sheet declines. So when rates go down, that could be bullish. Now, the trade-off is are they originating quickly on the front book versus the back book? So that matters too. And the front book is like new policies and what rates are coming in at and to what extent they've hedged their existing book of business with rates. So it depends, is the short summary. What we say — I was gonna say, get us a one-handed economist.

结束语

All right, so on that note, I hope that everybody enjoyed us on this Labor Day episode of Bits and Bips. So thank you as always. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. Until then, everyone.

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember nothing we say here is investment advice, and please check UnchainedCrypto.com/BitsAndBips for more disclosures. We'll be right back.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"反向 ADR"革命：这不是衍生品之争，而是资本主权之争
大多数人把 AMC vs Robinhood 之争看作"合规打架"，但真正被埋没的洞察是：**Robinhood 做的是一个"反向 ADR"（Reverse ADR）** —— 传统 ADR 是把外国股票包装进美国市场，而 Robinhood 是把美国股票包装出美国、送到全球。这个方向的翻转其实是二战后美元霸权逻辑在链上的镜像延续。
**一个让人意外的观察**：AMC CEO 骂 Robinhood 骂得越凶，AMC 股价越涨（一夜 21%）。这不是巧合，而是揭示了一个新的市场微观结构规律 —— **在 attention 经济里，被 tokenize 本身就是一种"上市二次 IPO"**。链上的 mimetic demand 会反哺链下股价。这与传统金融理论完全相反：传统认为衍生品是从标的派生价值，而在 meme + token 时代，**衍生层反过来给标的注入了"社交流动性溢价"**。Adam Aron 在骂人的同时，其实在给自己的股票做全球免费营销。
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 数据中心的政治困局

item.title: [Lex Clips] How agents are perfect for Linux | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"缺陷"的相变：Linux 悖论的反转时刻

DHH 提到的这个洞察其实是一场哲学级的反转：Linux 那些"过度具体、极度晦涩的错误信息"——过去二十年被视为它对普通用户最不友好的地方——在 AI 到来的瞬间从最大劣势变成了最大优势。

这里发生的不是"AI 帮我们读懂 Linux"，而是一次受众的悄然置换：错误信息的目标读者从人类变成了模型。当读者变了，同一段文本的"质量"评价就完全颠倒——对人越晦涩、对模型越具体、越能定位。Windows/macOS 那种"抱歉，出错了"式的友好错误，反而在 AI 时代变成了信息稀薄的负资产。

这让我想起一个跨领域的对照：基因组测序数据也曾是"垃圾"。ACGT 的四字母长串对人类完全不可读，被嘲笑为"没有信息的信息"。直到算力和模型追上来，这堆"乱码"才突然成了医学最珍贵的诊断金矿。Linux 的 stack trace 正在经历同样的相变——从噪声到信号的临界点，不在数据本身，而在读者的认知带宽。

二、多智能体的"意外副作用"：并发即混沌工程

DHH 顺口提了一句极其关键但没展开的话："当你同时跑多个 agent，它们会揪出你底层基础设施里所有那些人类手动操作从未触发过的竞态条件。"

这句话背后藏着一个反直觉的系统性真相：多智能体开发的最大价值可能根本不是"更快写代码"，而是意外成了一个永久在线的分布式压力测试。竞态条件是软件工程中最狡猾的一类 bug——它们只在特定并发时序下浮现，人类工程师几乎不可能靠手工重现。而 agent 群在正常工作时天然就是并发调用者，等于免费把 Netflix 的 Chaos Monkey 内嵌进了每一次日常开发。

跨领域连接：这与生态系统入侵物种的意外收益同构。一个物种进入新环境的"目的"从来不是暴露原生态位的脆弱性，但它的存在本身就是一场自然选择的实时体检。多智能体之于软件基础设施，等价于外来物种之于生态系统——不是它们要找 bug，是它们的存在方式就在找 bug。

三、被 GitHub 封禁的 bot：人类带宽校准的社会性基础设施正在崩溃

那个"12 秒提交 28 个 issue 被 GitHub 判为垃圾"的插曲，看似是小笑话，其实是一个时代级信号。

GitHub 的反垃圾阈值、API 速率限制、issue 模板规范——这些"社会性协议"全部按人类的思考与打字速度校准。当 agent 的产出速率把这些校准值撑爆，我们看到的不只是"技术摩擦"，而是整套围绕人类带宽建立的数字社会契约正在集体失灵。

这与 2010 年 5 月 6 日"闪崩"惊人相似：高频交易的速度撞碎了为人类交易员设计的市场微结构。市场并没有变得"更坏"，只是原来那些默默维持秩序的隐性假设——"下单速度大致等于人的反应速度"——被瞬间证伪。GitHub 的 spam filter 就是软件世界的 NYSE circuit breaker，它下一个必须被重新设计的假设是："issue 提交者是人"这条隐性前提。

四、最出人意料的一击：预发行 bug 报告与"未来时态"的软件工程

DHH 讲的那个 Mise 故事——bug 报告在软件还没发布之前就到了作者邮箱——是整段访谈里最容易被忽略但最颠覆的时刻。

传统软件工程的因果链是：发布 → 用户遇到问题 → 提交 issue → 修复。这个链条的时间箭头一直朝前。而 agent 能够去读未发行代码、模拟运行、预判问题——它把因果链倒过来了：问题在成为问题之前就被报告。

这在物理学上有个精确的对应：从被动观测宇宙 → 主动做粒子对撞实验。前者只能等宇宙自己产生现象，后者主动制造现象。Agent 让每一个开发者都从"等用户报 bug 的观测者"升级为"主动对撞未来场景的实验者"。而 Shopify 的那个研究更是钉死了这件事——agent 审查过的 PR 在生产环境里造成的问题更少——这已经不是"AI 能不能调试"的问题了，而是人类审查员正在从最后防线变成质量的瓶颈。

一个更让人心里一震的推论：如果 agent 能在软件"存在"之前就报告它的 bug，那么"软件版本"这个概念本身可能正在失效。版本号是为人类的记忆和沟通设计的，不是为持续演化的代码库设计的。Mise 需要一天更新七次这件事，只是这个更深变化的第一声回响。

📝 转录文本

Linux + Agents: A Perfect Match

I think this, by the way, is one of the other breakthroughs that is going to lead to the total domination of Linux.

The agents have taken all of the hardship out of diagnosing Linux systems and turned the fact that Linux produces these overly specific, totally arcane error messages into its greatest advantage.

When Linux has an issue, the agent can take that very specific error message that makes no sense to a normal human and correlate it with the fact that the agent was pre-trained on 40 million lines of Linux code, so it knows exactly where to look and dial it down.

I have not had a single problem on my Linux machine since the beginning of this year that an agent could not diagnose. That was not true a year and a half ago. A year and a half ago, I was still searching on forums to find answers to esoteric questions.

Now, the agents know the source code of not just the Linux operating system, but every single piece of software I have on that box. The agent has access to the source code of all of it.

The Crash Watcher in Omakub Quattro

In fact, this was one thing I built in just before we shipped. So, once you set up your default agent, Omakub Quattro has a crash watcher. If any app on your machine crashes, it'll pop up a little thing, ask you whether you want your AI to diagnose the problem.

Yeah. That's amazing. Unbelievable.

I've seen things where there's an error in some subsystem — some not even Linux, just some app I installed — the agent starts digging through the logs and looks up systemd log, then it checks out the damn source code of the application that crashed, pins down that it's in this Rust file line 472 that there's an unbounded, unwrapped variable that overflowed or whatever it is. Then, offers you whether you want to file a bug report with all this detail.

The Mise Story: An Amazing Anecdote

I'll give you one amazing anecdote.

So, I was working with um this guy JDX who's working on Mise. This is this package manager for uh fast-moving development tools. This is how we manage all the agent software and so forth. Normal package managers are not built to be updated seven times a day.

[snorts]

And all of these agent harnesses are updated about seven times a day. So, we needed an out-of-band uh package manager, and Mise just turns out to be perfect for this.

Anyway, it had a small bug. There was some uh race condition — which agents are very good at finding, because when you start running multiple agents at the same time, they will suss out all these race conditions you have in your underlying infrastructure that was never triggered by a human trying to do manual thing.

Banned by GitHub for Spam

So, it finds this issue, right? I tell um I tell the agent, "Hey, um can you post this as a bug report to JDX's uh GitHub?"

And unfortunately, right before that, I had had to do a QA run on Omakub itself with eight different agents. It had found 28 real issues that it needed to file. Well, it went to GitHub and tried to file all 28 issues at the same time, which it did in about uh I don't know, 12 seconds.

GitHub, not unreasonably, marked that as probable spam and banned my Omakub bot. And then I couldn't do that. So, I was blocked from the bot having access to GitHub.

So, I just told it, "Hey, you know what? Just email JDX. Here's his email address." I had already set it up with hey.com, an email address. We have a CLI that's in beta right now. So, I set it up with that so it can send the email. That's how it gives me reports about outstanding issues and PRs.

A Bug Report Before the Release

So, it sends JDX this email about the bug it found. And he was like, "Wait, this is the first time I've gotten a bug report in unreleased software." Because it had downloaded the source code to Mise, saw that he had already fixed a bug but that it would not fix the problem entirely in software that had not shipped yet.

Yeah.

Pinpointed the problem. And he was like, "Damn it, I got a bug report before we even cut a release."

Unbelievable — AGI levels of mind-blowing stuff.

Can Agents Actually Debug? The Shopify Study

And that was actually — if you remember — that was an open question, whether AI assistants could debug well. That was kind of the thought that, yeah sure, they can write code, but can they find issues?

They are so incredibly good at this. And this is actually interesting, because I was on the perhaps same side of that — a little skeptical about, can it reason about all these things?

And Mikhail, who's the CTO at Shopify, ran a scientific study on this. They had — and this was I think late last year or early this year — where he had agents go back through all the incidents, both outages and other problems that Shopify had had in production, trace that back to the PR that was merged, and find out whether the PRs that had been reviewed by human or PRs that had been reviewed by agents were of higher quality.

Well, lo and surprise, the —

[clears throat]

— the PRs that had been reviewed by agents caused fewer issues in production. And this was with models we had 6 months ago.

At this point, 100%, in the majority of domains we work in today, agents are better at finding bugs.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Business of Sport] Does the British Media Hate Successful People | James Haskell
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：Haskell 其实是"英国媒体逻辑"最完美的产物，而不是受害者

他花大量时间抱怨英国媒体如何"捧杀"名人、如何嫉妒成功者。但仔细听他的叙述会发现一个悖论——他的所有商业成功（书籍、播客、代言、DJ 事业）恰恰是建立在"被误解"这一情感杠杆上的。他自己说了："我一周会收到三四次'我以前觉得你是个混蛋，现在改观了'的私信。"

这意味着："先被讨厌"是他商业模式的入口漏斗。如果英国媒体真的像美国媒体那样对成功者友好，Haskell 就没有那个"人格反转"的戏剧曲线可以卖了。他愤怒地抱怨的那个系统，正是他所有非橄榄球收入的定价机制。这就像鱼在抱怨水太湿——他把生存环境错认成了敌人。

跨领域连接：橄榄球的溃败 = 传统媒体的溃败 = 同一种"业余治理精英主义"的病

他讲的那个 RFU（英格兰橄榄球联盟）故事有一个让人震惊的细节：理事会成员被要求投票决定是否解散自己的职位。他们当然否决了。 这不是橄榄球的问题，这是一个跨越所有百年机构的通用病理：

  • BBC、《卫报》等传统媒体也是被"业余治理者"（60 岁以上、不理解社交媒体、以"传统"为身份认同）把持
  • 大学的终身教职委员会
  • 大多数国家的中央银行治理结构
  • 医学专业协会

Haskell 无意间描述的是"自我延续型精英治理"的通用溃败模式：一个组织当它的治理层由"以'守护传统'为身份"的业余者组成时，这个组织无法进行任何威胁到治理层身份的改革。你看到的不是橄榄球病了，你看到的是任何以"业余精神"为道德优越性的机构，在专业化经济中都必然崩溃。 Full Contact 被 Netflix 砍掉这件事之所以成为完美的隐喻，是因为它揭示了：这些机构宁愿死，也不愿被看见真实的自己。

隐藏的系统性真相：Haskell 的整个人生哲学是一个"疼痛货币化"引擎

注意他讲话的节奏和主题的隐藏结构： - 身体（10 万英镑修复、睾酮从 3 恢复到 25） - 童年（父亲的操纵、17 岁开始的治疗） - 职业（受骗签约、被低薪、诉讼 68 万英镑） - 关系（离婚、父亲留下的财务烂摊子）

大多数运动员在退役后会尽力掩藏这些伤口。Haskell 做的完全相反——他把每一次疼痛都转化成了一个内容产品：书、演讲、播客话题、纪录片素材。

这里有个惊人的洞察：他其实是英国最早期的"创伤经济"从业者之一，只是他自己没意识到。他反复说的那句"你可以骗所有人，但骗不了自己"——这不仅是他父亲的教诲，这是内容经济时代的核心资产。在一个"真实性 = 稀缺性"的注意力市场里，愿意公开承认自己被父亲坑了 10 万英镑的前橄榄球国脚，比一百个完美的品牌大使更有价值。

他抱怨自己"没坐过私人飞机"——但真正的问题不是他赚得不够多，而是他还没有意识到自己已经从"橄榄球运动员"进化成了一个"人格 IP 运营者"，而后者的定价模型完全不同。 他还在用运动员的账本算内容创业者的收入。这就是他"下一个突破"的所在位置。

身体的代价：伤病、手术与 10 万英镑的自费维修

主持人：Can I ask, how broken is your body?

Haskell：Pretty broken, yeah. From my perspective, I'm not one of these rugby players that at this point in time — touch wood — that I have any sort of cerebral issues or mental issues. I played a very physical position and my approach to my training and the way I worked was very, very intense. A lot of my teammates and coaches would say I was one of the most professional players they'd seen in terms of nutrition, training, working with other people, accessing other sports, talking to different individuals.

I reinvested a lot in myself, so I never accepted what the club offered me wherever I was. I'd always get my own physio, own nutritionist. I would do what they wanted me to do, but I would always think there was a better answer.

Because if you look at the NFL, for example — if you're paying Patrick Mahomes 450 million over 10 years, if he breaks down, that is a massive issue, and they have high level quality of staff and people to look after. If the best rugby player in your squad is paid — I mean today it's slightly different — but say paid 350, 400 grand a year, the budgets of a medical and everything else like that are not the highest. So you're not going to get access to the best people. Sometimes you do have amazing people, but often you'll get some average care.

And so having finished playing, I've had probably four or five operations since I retired. I had a discectomy on my back, I had a screw taken out my wrist, I had my bicep reattached, I had my ankle cleaned out, and then I ultimately had my ankle fused about a year ago. I'll get no insurance to pay for it — all myself. I reckon I've done probably 100 grand on injections, physio, medical fees, pilates. I've tried Ayurveda, Reiki — I've tried everything. Even when I went to Fiji, I saw something about my ankle, like a witch doctor. He wrapped my foot in leaves. I'll do anything to feel better.

But I've always — I see a wellness doctor, I work with a testosterone company. I had my testosterone test the other day: it was three. It starts at a healthy level about 12. So I was really low. I'd obviously shot myself to pieces with kind of training and tiredness. So I've got that back up to about 25.

I've always looked to get my bloods done. So everything I do is science-based information. It's not gym wisdom where a meathead says, oh, you want to take this. Because like anything in life, the cheque's always in the post. If you drink and smash it up now, it's not now you're going to worry about — it's when you're older. When you smoke now, it's not a problem, it's when you're older.

So my body's pretty wrecked, and sometimes having a low level of pain in my back, my neck, my ankles, my feet — waking up, feel like you've been hit or been put through a tumble dryer. But I do look after myself.

Travis Allen 的教训：训练太多，比赛太少

I would say my biggest thing about my performance was doing too much off the field by extra training. I remember it quite clearly. We had this meeting at High Road House in London. He said, "I want to sit through and go through a game with you." 父亲的教诲：你可以骗所有人，但骗不了自己

And my dad taught me a very valuable lesson when I was younger, which was: you can lie to everyone else, but you can't lie to yourself. And when someone says, for example, you've got a drink problem, or you're late, or you're lazy, or you're tired, or you don't behave, or you're not a good parent — you can listen to it and you can have all the excuses. But that moment when perhaps when you go to bed, when you switch your phone off just before you close your eyes, everything hits you. And then you're like, maybe there's a bit of truth in this.

And that happened twice in my career at that point. And also, the day before my first day at Wasps, my dad said to me, "I know you don't like tackling. You're a bit of a fucking pussy. You don't tackle properly. You tackle up high, you're going to get found out if you don't learn to tackle properly." I was like, shut up, dad. Anyway, I had a row.

Went into Wasps next day and I was like, he's right. I don't really like this, I'm technically not very good at it. And I went up to Joe Worsley, who I regard as the best tackler in the world. I said, "Joe, nice to meet you." And he thought my name was Jonathan, which is my dad's name, for the first three months. I didn't have the balls to tell him it was something different. So he said, "Lawrence Delalia." I went, "Joe, his name's James." And Joe looks at me: "Why don't you tell me?" I was like, "I'm sorry, sir."

I went up to him, said, "Listen, I can't really tackle. You're the best tackler I've ever seen. Come with practice every day." For nine and a half seasons, I practiced my tackling, bar team run days or game days. But I would practice it, and it became one of my greatest assets, and I became a very physically dominant player. Was that necessary in my nature? Not really.

Same thing with this conversation with Travis. I went away and I was like, "You're right." So I said, "Listen, I've lost my way." I was probably, I don't remember, maybe 40-odd caps or 50 caps at the time. Help me or talk to me about something. So we worked on it, and that was just before I toured Australia, where I played what people perceive as my best rugby for England. And then I went on the Lions tour, and it completely changed the way I did things.

So I had to listen and I had to have self-awareness and also put your ego in check. And because of all the therapy and all that kind of stuff, I go from day to day. If I can't control it, I don't worry about it. I don't overthink things.

I've worked very hard, particularly from the start of this year, on doing what I did when I played. If you've got negative thoughts, concerns and fears, sit. You can change your thinking, visualisation — all these really important elements. And I just sit in the day. Like last night, I knew what I was doing today. I woke up this morning, did what I need to do. I haven't looked at tomorrow. I haven't looked at what I did yesterday. I'm on it today.

And so Sam's mindset about those compromises — no, look, going to France is hard. They train you hard. It's a bit mad over there. It's Wild West. It can be quite political in terms of what they do in coaching and clubs, and they're very passionate. But actually, if you have the mentality I had, you just live in the present. So I never concerned myself.

主持人：It does hurt me though.

Haskell：Don't look at it. It doesn't matter. Who cares? You don't know him. If I tell you — so two things I thought were interesting. Noel Gallagher said — well, three things. Henry Ford, who invented the car, he said: if you'd asked people at that time what they wanted, they would have said a faster horse, not a car. So they gave him a car — he don't need a horse anymore.

Noel Gallagher said: nobody wanted Oasis. No one gave him Oasis — they wanted something else. Who cares what they want, give them what you believe in and test it. And obviously, if there is some popularity, stick with what you do.

And Tom Holland, Spider-Man, said that if you've got a problem with him or a comment with him, text him. And if you haven't got his number, you don't know him well enough to text him.

I do not give a shit about people's comments. Now, does it still hurt if you see them or people talk about them? 100%. Because we're programmed like that. People who say, "I don't care about other people's opinions" — of course you do. But I don't look, because it's a form of self-harm.

If you believe in what you're saying, then you shouldn't worry about people who haven't met you, who aren't informed, who have no context. Social media does not work because it takes all the context away. How could you relate to somebody who's a single mother of three from a different country, who has had no money — you're never going to. Whose political background is very different, who sees the world in a completely different space. You're not meant to. That's why it's caused more agg than anything else, because contextually we have no background, no knowledge, no understanding.

So when you put stuff out there, if you say, "I like milk, I love cow's milk," people go, "How fucking dare you? You're destroying the environment. What about almond milk? You shouldn't drink milk." You're like, I just said I like milk. Relax.

So I post now, I don't look. And I've got a video guy that does stuff with me and I go, look, if you said something outlandish, or something that is provably wrong, then you've got to step back and put your hand up and say, "I've got that wrong." But what people want or don't want — the fact they're commenting is brilliant, because you want now to create interaction.

And every time I do something, I want people — because that's what life's like — to equally like or dislike me. If people have no reaction to you, what are you doing in life? It's creating conversation. Negative or positive is brilliant.

高罂粟综合症：英国如何对待成功的运动员

主持人：Unlike so many rugby players, you actually built a profile and a personality away from rugby. And one of our big challenges to rugby, whenever we've had people sitting down here, was: guys, the sport fucking needs people. They're boring. They transcend the boundaries of just the sport. So you need to be able to go out into different industries. You need to get other people to care. But for you, being able to do that while also playing — did that change how the perception was in the dressing room for you? Was it harder? Because everyone says, "Oh no, look, stick your head above the parapet, it's about the team, you can't be the individual."

Haskell：In my perspective, there was lots of things probably that I didn't get right to start with. And the most important thing as a sports person in this country — you have to understand the media and the person in the street. We've got a bit of tall poppy syndrome. We're actually not that happy for people to do well over here at all.

America, American dream society, is built on people doing well and wanting to support you. Our media is built on criticism and destruction. People love to gossip over here and go, "Fucking hell, so-and-so thinks he's better than he is." And that all bubbles away in the corner.

Now, so you have to back it up with performances. You look at guys like Mayweather. I wouldn't advocate necessarily how he conducts himself outside the ring, but he was a showman and the way he did everything, he created a character. You look at someone like Canelo — unbelievable boxer, but doesn't really say anything, doesn't do anything. Mayweather will always be seen as that kind of bigger athlete. Muhammad Ali, same. Michael Jordan on The Last Dance — not one person said he was good, they liked him. Everyone said incredible teammate, unbelievable athlete, leader. And he did things his way and transcended the sport.

The problem with sportsmen in the UK is if you do well and you put your head above the parapet, that's fine, but you better fucking back it up. How many people were so keen to see Conor McGregor get filled in? Because he made other people uncomfortable.

Because you've got to remember that successful people with personality — multidimensional — shine a light on your own inadequacies. You are reflected. It makes people uncomfortable, because a lot of people like to be average. Some people were born, will be born, get a job, and it won't be a career, it's a job. They will have a family and that's all they'll ever do. And they're very happy with that.

When someone goes, "I am almost like a polyglot. I've got a million things under my belt. I deal with this kind of stuff. I've got a personality. You're good-looking. You're funny. You're gregarious" — people want to see you fail.

And our media is the worst media in the world. Every celeb or every sportsman says it, because they'll build you up and then they will go out of their way to fuck you over and crush you. And then we like to raise you up again and then we crush you again. America is a very different ballgame. Now, with the advent of social media and TMZ and all that kind of stuff, it is going a bit more that way. But I do think sports — having a personality is important.

更衣室的接纳：Good Bad Rugby 上的自证

And I felt that no one in the changing room ever got in the way. Like some lads, you could see… I'll put it this way: we had on Good Bad Rugby a podcast, we could probably go about nine seasons now, and under the guise of House Rugby before that. Most people in my team, in my career, came on — including coaches and people, some of the most dour coaches in the world who you thought would absolutely hate me because I was the antithesis of everything they were about. Because I worked hard, because I was a good team man, because I was super professional, they love me.

Most guys went, "Before I met James Haskell, I want to punch him in the face." That's why they all came on the show. All of them. "I thought he was a dick." I've seen it with all of them. I see their body language straight away. I go, you think you know me. You've seen my naked calendars for the Jeans for Genes. You've seen me DJing. You've seen me making music. You've seen me doing funny skits. You think I'm a prick.

They then meet me and go, "He's still a prick, but he's a good one. And I don't want to punch him in the face less." And they all say it.

Everything that's ever been written about me is always the same tripe that is basically misunderstood, actually this and this. It's because you don't know me and you're judging everything. And I get messages now, I'd say three or four times a week: "I saw you on this. I used to think you were a prick, but I really like you. I saw you on that. You've completely changed my opinion. I saw you talk about your mental health — wow, how brave. Completely different than I thought you were." It's like, you didn't know me. You never met me. You just did what we all do.

Which is: when you read an article about Kim Kardashian, you go, "I can't believe fucking hell, what's she doing?" And then when you appear in the newspaper and you know it's tripe and they've made it up, you go, "I can't believe it, outrage." But human nature is to judge books by its cover.

And particularly in this country, we do not have that "I want to see you do well." It's hard. We have this inherent jealousy. And because of the way things are structured, we like to fit our sports people into boxes: have a personality, not too much; be humble, but…

That's why, when it works really well, like Harry Kane — incredible talent, but he's not the greatest media personality in the world, really. But I don't know. He probably, if he had the shackles off — but the intensity that football players have to go under. He is, for me, a great leader, an unbelievable player, seems like a really good guy, good family guy. Would you want to have a personality if every time you did it, you're criticised? And bear in mind, football fans are bordering on the most passionate. And when I mean passionate, for a lot of people, it's an escapism from their real life, sport, particularly football. 主持人：By a sports group, Tom Boa?

Rugby — posts, field, kit — it's more complicated. Sevens, easier to do, really.

Full Contact 的失败：橄榄球最大的自毁

But I do think with rugby, if you want to understand how rugby does rugby: Full Contact, Netflix, right? You have the perfect vehicle. F1 before Drive to Survive was diminishing. Couldn't access a younger audience. Drive to Survive came and they showed the fights, the battles, the swearing, the rule breaks, the teamwork, the trials, the technology, the routines, the characters, the people.

Now in life, because of social media, it's not just watching the event. They want to know what you're like, what you're doing behind the scenes, what your family's like, what kind of parent you are, what you go on holiday, what you drive, what you eat. That's why At Home with the Furys — it's not just him. It's him and his kids and his wife. People want to know. That's why Quarterbacks on Netflix — it can't just be three or four of the best quarterbacks. Everyone wants to know what they're like. What do they do with their missus? How are they at home? What events? What do they drink? What do they go out? That's where life's going. We want to look behind the curtain.

So against all the odds, rugby had an opportunity with Full Contact on Netflix, right? To suddenly — with all the other stuff, the tennis and everything else that had been developed — to make something mega.

And all we did was squabble about what we're being paid. I don't know what the fees were, but you know, "We're not going to do it, do it." Everyone was so worried about cameras in the rooms. The team, a lot of these coaches — again, don't have social media, never done social media, don't have media training, aren't really interested. "It's all about the team." What was the fear? "We need editorial approval." And then we do one season. I never watched it, but it was pretty boring. They got a second season. They cancelled the second season before the first season had even come out.

We managed to fuck up the greatest opportunity rugby had to transform its worries because somebody was worried that someone might have "changed" them — see, you call someone a see-you-in-T or do something.

And what rugby forgets is: in life, in anything, the silence you leave, the void you leave, people will fill it with opinions and thoughts and everything else. Show them it. Show them the rawness. I've just watched a video today of Pep Guardiola talking about Kevin De Bruyne and having to let him go. He's on to tears. The rawness. How can you let a player that's done 10 seasons at Man City, scored over 100 goals, 140 assists or whatever he's done, and have all this kind of stuff? Then you know why rugby can't do that. You wouldn't let have the cameras in the changing rooms.

Rugby turned the greatest opportunity and balls it up to the point where they cancelled it before the second season even came out. And that is all you ever need to know about rugby. If you ever want to know what rugby's like, is: rugby doing rugby, getting themselves cancelled, boring, putting on events that no one watches, that no one cares about, because they don't know what they're doing.

Court case — I realised that our lawyers, every time they sent an email to me, Mike and Alex were charging us because we were sued as three individuals, not as a company. Every time responded, they were charging us. So I kept saying to them, "Listen, we're not made of money. Do not think this is a cash cow. So they basically stopped messaging me, just started dealing with Alex. They then told Alex halfway through that it was going to go because 750,000, not 250,000. Never told us. Never wrote to us client care letters, said they were going to do it. We managed to get security of costs against them, went all the way through to the end, and the day before court, they pulled out. And obviously in UK law, you can't counter. So we either had a choice: do we pursue them, or do we just take our ball home and do we just deal with whatever they want? I think we had to give an apology — some bullshit that we did.

And then the answer was, we then had a bill of 750 grand. Which we thought the new company we were working with had been servicing the bill. Turns out Alex was getting calls every day because we owed him 500 grand and no one had paid it. I said, "Alex, I'll deal with this." Called him up with one call and said, "Stop calling him. There's no money. You're hounding him. Let's stop calling." I said, "Well, you should have sent me in there anyway."

We then had to fire our lawyers, our own lawyers, because they had not told us. So it's like me coming around to your house going, "Could you prune my rose bushes, which I imagine you've got? Could you do this? Could you don't do the topiary on the extensive lawn — right, on the bushes?" And then building your swimming pool and coming back over: "You I'm a million quid for swimming pool." You're like, "I didn't order a swimming pool." "Like we've built it now." And that's basically what they did. They never told us what they were doing.

So me and Mike, I explained: if you could show us what you told us it was going to go out, money will pay. Luckily, the business made that money. But Alex almost had a nervous breakdown. It almost destroyed our relationship with other people.

But the podcast basically launched and became profitable and has carried on. So we've gone from the phoenix in the flames, through the ashes, had all this drama. I've been cancelled twice doing it. Unfortunately, I'm bright in certain ways, in social situations. I'm relatively articulate. I'm a good learner. I don't have that business — I'm not great with figures. So I know my limitations. I work with people that do. And obviously, because of the way I've conducted myself, not intentionally, I'm not always the most brand-friendly person. If you want to be the family and friends brand, they're not going to come to you. But that's great. You know what you want.

Also, I don't want to ever pretend to be something I'm not, because you get caught out. If you read in the papers that James Haskell's sworn and done something and pushed someone down the stairs, you go, "Oh, that sounds probably a bit like him." It's when someone goes, "Oh, my God, you know, James Haskell" — I'm like, they're hugging babies and kissing children, and then suddenly you get found out. James Haskell's seen with almond milk. You're like, "What? What a guy. I feel betrayed."

But again, I think for me with a lot of this stuff, it is challenging and I do have those moments of woe. But I have worked so hard recently on trying to reframe things and trying to understand this. And look, there are times when stuff really gets on top of you. But again, I try to have the emotional reaction, which you should be entitled to — kick your toys, throw your pram, swear, lost, desperate, "What am I going to do?" And then you've got to go, "Look, there's got to be a way out of it." And sometimes there isn't. And sometimes you have to take your medicine.

But I think ultimately, if you go back again to what you can control, who can help you, how can you get help, and what's the plan to get you out of where you're going to go. And also talking about having an open mind, being positive, and going, "Look, there is…" Because we can always complain about stuff. Be grateful for what you've got, not what you haven't got. Because you're only fighting against yourself. And I know it sounds like rhetoric you'd hear online, but it is true. I'm as happy as ever with a good cup of coffee, mate. What's the problem?

And we get on very well together. We've had a couple of rows over stuff, but actually, I think I'm a very good judge of character. And a lot of people that I called out with these guys — I'm not going to sit on here, but we've been stitched up on a couple of things where I told these guys, "I told them point blank, lads. You are going to get…" Because I basically said, "I don't trust them. I don't care. Until you put a contract, shareholding agreement thing, I'm not interested in doing it. I'm not having my word." Take my word. Don't take anyone's word. I trust no one. Really. I see human nature for exactly what it is. Before someone to a corner, they'll do whatever they need to do. And people, if they can get away with it, we'll show, after you cheat and whatever.

So I said to him, and lo and behold, the lads got fucked. And we all three of us got fucked by somebody or something. It's like, "Lads, you've got to play nice and be respectful, but ultimately you have to do what needs to be done." So I think we do get on really well, and actually we're able to have conversations. But we are three very different people with three different experiences. But we love what we do. We love the audience that we've got. We love talking and having the passion, and it doesn't ever feel like work and it's never a chore.

The only time it was a chore was the court case and trying to manage other people we work with. And as soon as you get to business, you've got staff. Staff's the biggest issue for any business, because no one cares about your business as much as you do. And you've got to go through — kiss a lot of frogs to find a prince or princess that's prepared to work hard and do what needs to be done.

And this modern generation, they want it all for nothing and don't want to work, aren't prepared to commit, don't want to work weekends, aren't prepared to sacrifice. And people say to me, "Well, it's different for you." Why? Why am I different? I have an argument with producers. "Oh, can you come in here?" I was like, "No, I've got to take my daughter to school. I've got to do this." "Well, you know, what other people can." I mean, here's my diary. Turn my laptop around. "Look at that. Look what I did." "Well, I've never seen anything like it."

This is life. You either meet me or we don't do it. And he goes, "Well, I'm working on weekends." "Well, I'm 0-0-0." "What do you fucking mean you're 0-0-0? I'm representing the business. Why is there no one from our business working? Why am I going to a GBR event and no one I can get hold of?" It's not how it works. You work and you work hard and you do what needs to be done. Now, you need to get work-life balance. But if you're not prepared to work and sacrifice, I'll find someone else who is.

"Oh, you can't do that because you can't fire anyone these days. You can't tell anyone the shit. You've got to go, 'What do you stop doing, start doing, keep doing? Here's a formal letter.'" I understand about employment, but there needs to be some protection over some things.

But I think the issue is that, like in life, in a friendship group — I said to you earlier, there's always people that are going to pull together, help you, and be good energy givers or energy sappers. Same thing with business. There are people that see this as a career and want to work, but there are people who are 9-to-5ers, or nine-to-threes, and that's all they want to do. And you're like, fine, but that's not what I want. Just because you don't want to meet me halfway, I'm not here to listen to you or stop you. Go at your pace, you work at my pace. You can't take the pace, go away. And that's what I believe in all this stuff.

一周的节奏：混乱、结构与享受

I think when I was a player with all the stuff I did, I probably got the work-life balance wrong a little bit. So I had to run it back, had to listen to Travis, do less, be better for weekends, peak at the right times. Did I go through the openings of envelopes? Did I go and meet everyone that would have a coffee with me to talk about business? Was a lot of it a waste of time? Could have been an email, could have been a Zoom. Yeah. Now I'm ruthless on all that stuff.

But life's for living and fun. I was in France for a week. I flew back to London on Saturday night, DJed on my own event I did in Shoreditch from 2 till 11 with some guest DJs, flew back to France Monday. I had a France all week, flew back Sunday, took my ex-wife and my daughter for food, DJed Sunday night, woke up at five, got home at 12, woke up at five, flew to Toulouse, interviewed Antoine Dupont, did an Adidas campaign, flew back Tuesday, had work, here today, two DJ sets. And I've got all the admin work bits, stuff. I've got a PA, I've got stuff to help me. But that's how I want to live my life.

I like the chaos, I like the structure, I like doing it. I've got Thursday, Friday, two days with my daughter, just focused on her. I'm taking her, I'm going to physio, she'll come with me, I'll take her for food, I'll play with her, all that stuff. Saturday, Sunday, I play with her all day, DJ sets balance. That's me, that's balance. That's how I want to do it. I don't want to be sitting at home, I don't want to retire, I just want to keep working. So when I go to a restaurant, I can have a bottle of Montrachet and enjoy myself, or have a Cohiba Robusto and enjoy myself, and that's it. And I'm prepared to do it.

快问快答：品牌、嘉宾、球员与遗憾

主持人：Should we do a quickfire round? What brand do you not work with today that you would most like to work with?

Haskell：Oh, that is a very good question. AP, I quite like. I'm not a big watch man. I like my watches, but the Royal Oak — there's a rose gold and black one that I think is fantastic. It's big. They've got big watches. Arnold Schwarzenegger used to wear it. They've got big ones. Their feet suit me. I think they're really cool.

I would love to — I don't think it'd be great for my health, but the Cohiba brand, a cigar brand, stuff like that. Because I do like that. Someone said, "Oh, you can't talk about smoking. You shouldn't put it out there." Well, whatever. Arnie used to do it. So why not? The Rock smokes. So I think AP would be right up there.

主持人：Favourite person you've spoken to on GBR?

Haskell：Oh, I've had some amazing ones. I thought Jason Fox I really enjoy. Bobby Skinstad, he was great. And Eddie Jones, I think. They're all up there because they're all very different. Because that's the beauty of the show is one day it's emotional. Like when Nigel Owens came on, he talked about him trying to take his own life. I've known him for years and the question of his sexuality and stuff. And you just think, that's how terrible, how difficult that would have been. And next week you're then laughing with Billy Vunipola or something else. I love the rollercoaster.

主持人：Who did you most dislike playing against? Could be feared, could be fucking nightmare to mark. Individual players.

Haskell：Any massive Polynesian or sort of Pacific Islander — it was always going to be a tough day in the afternoon. Guys like — I remember the biggest hit I ever got hit on me was Sam Tuitupou, who played for the All Blacks and played for Sale. Hit me. I wasn't even looking, hit me and basically put my ribs through the other side of my head. The fridge with legs. Yeah. Henry Tuilagi — you always knew that I was going to be, I played Sevens once against Henry Tuilagi. I mean, there's a lot of space for a huge man, and like trying to tackle him around the leg. So that was always quite tricky. Any of those guys, you just knew that it was going to be a tough afternoon and that you're about to get levelled.

主持人：What have you not done yet that you'd like to?

Haskell：What have I not done? I've never been on a private jet.

主持人：What? No, no.

Haskell：Sorry, brother. I'm a former rugby player. I'm not — I know I come across…

主持人：Listen.

Haskell：What? I'm divorced. Listen, I'm divorced. I have to earn a lot of money. I've got fucking two houses, one and a half houses to pay for. Cars, things, everything. Divorce, bits, travel. I need to earn more. I need to earn way more than I'm earning. I've got a Range Rover, but then some drug dealer crashed into me the other day with my daughter in the car, snapped the wheel off and then legged it. But luckily he was insured. And he got arrested. He was an insured drug dealer.

主持人：Yeah, mental, conscientious, isn't it? Road safety.

Haskell：Less likely to get pulled over.

主持人：Less likely to get pulled over, exactly.

Haskell：Yeah, because that's how stupid it would be if you've got like a gram of gear in the car, you get pulled over for not insuring. Like a moron.

主持人：You have your opinions, you're confident in yourself. Is there anything that you regret?

Haskell：Oh, good question. There was something I regretted the other day, actually, I thought. I'd rather let my dad manage me at the time — only because he didn't have any experience and I think he probably created part of the myth around Brand Haskell and all that kind of stuff that wasn't me. I'm actually not as big a prick as people think I am. So that I think would probably be something I wish I hadn't done, because it changed our relationship. Even though I still loved him at the end and we knew he loved it. I made the conscious choice to look past everything just because you only get one dad. So that wasn't a problem. When he passed away, I was very content and I knew he loved me. So that wasn't a problem and vice versa. But I think him managing, I think, what else would I have not done? I think I'd say that one.

I think most things, regrets — I don't give a lot of time for it. There's things that I cringe at that I've done. I'm like, "Oh, why did I do that?"

主持人：What goes through your mind then?

Haskell：I don't know, just some ways I dressed before and I turned up and like, I don't know. Yeah, just little bits. But mostly I'm pretty happy because everything shaped me to be the person I am today. And again, when I said about, when things get tough, I always think that if you are so focused on what you want and what's happening, you actually step back and go: if I'm receptive and open and happy, things fall into lap. I find when I'm like that, stuff, people knock on my door, connections — and what you're doing is it's not what you wanted it to be. You want two million quid deal, but then we actually looked at it, if you were present, you go, "Oh, that adds to that and that and that's coming," and before you know it, you're actually in a good place. And so I've tried to do a lot more of that and not regret stuff too much.

营养建议、素食主义者与 Padel

主持人：If you could only give someone one piece of nutrition advice, what would it be?

Haskell：Worry about your protein, always. Where's your protein source coming from? It should be the most important part of every meal. If you look at your plate and you can't see where your protein is, you're fucked before you even start it.

主持人：Don't go vegan.

Haskell：Not for that. Well, I mean, vegan — I wouldn't, because it doesn't work for everyone and the amount of supplementation you have to have. And I also think the best meals are medically improving — animal proteins with plant-based as well. So I would have plant-based food. I would try lots of things. I'd have variety. Always colour on your plate. Not one is better than the other. And everyone thinks about The Game Changers. People were winning way more Olympic medals ever than not being a vegan. It's like, "Look how amazing these people are doing it." I was like, "Yeah, but they were doing it, lots of other people are doing loads of other things."

主持人：So I wonder what they're worst… You can just say you dislike vegans.

Haskell：I don't. I like vegans. Some of my best friends are vegans. I probably know more about veganism than anyone else. Them and Hyrox people, you know all about them, because they fucking don't show up.

主持人：You never do Hyrox?

Haskell：No, not because I don't like — dislike a brand. It's just I can't run. My ankle fused and I don't want to run around doing stuff like that.

主持人：So you haven't fallen down the padel train either?

Haskell：No, I've played padel. I've not seen a little boy on the TV show — a vegan and a vegetarian run off a cliff — who hits the ground first, or who wins? Who wins? Society. Sorry, but padel — yeah, I love padel. I've had six lessons, played four times. Love it. For a bigger gentleman, want to play more.

主持人：Six lessons played four times? It's not great.

Haskell：No. So six padel lessons played four actual games.

主持人：Not — you to the slowest, the classes you're right, you know?

Haskell：Too literal. Yeah, exactly. Too literal, just cut the nerds loving life. Well, one super nerd, one front-of-house. The front-of-house nerd. Yeah, less nerds, more palatable. Well, what more money are you earning? Get back in there, wait until the fucking deal's signed.

想采访的人、结束语与 OnlyFans 玩笑

主持人：Who have you not had on the pod who you'd most like to have on?

Haskell：Oh, I really want to interview — guys like Ricky Gervais I want to really speak to. The Rock, I think, would be great. And Arnie. I think his business acumen — look at Rock in terms of all the stuff he touches, how smart he is. For America, he swears a bit. He's a bit edgy. Nothing bad, but he's just a big character and I love it. He's gone from Arnie, weightlifter from Austria, to governor of California. That's stuff that people write in books. That's stuff people write in dream journals that never happens. Tindall's — Wakefield to Windsor. From Corgis to Coalmines. Oh, Coalmines to Corgis. That's unheard of.

Rock — from wrestling to the highest-paid movie star of all time, selling brands, bits, millions and millions and millions of pounds. Interesting guy, kept his personality, seems to be a great, good family man. Like, really interesting.

主持人：James, dude, you've been amazing. I think we should go on a private jet.

Haskell：Yes. Can we make some money together?

主持人：I don't know how to do it.

Haskell：Yeah, yeah. You sound like you've got enough, so just share it around. How can I make some more? Because I need it.

主持人：As I'm hungry, what do you need to do?

Haskell：I'm not doing anything too… Well, on that note, follow James' OnlyFans.

主持人：It's out of action. Shut that down.

Haskell：Follow me on Instagram. If you like music, you can follow me on SoundCloud. I've got a Facebook page. I'm not — cross-heading under James Haskell or Haskell Music. Very simple. Buy my books. What a Flanker. Ruck Me. What a Flanker. Basically What a Flanker. Ruck Me. I've written another book.

主持人：No, I did get it. Well, you say that. You shouldn't laugh as loud as I needed you to.

Haskell：How much money did you make out of it?

主持人：A lot. Not a lot. Not as much as I should have.

Haskell：Dude, you're a star.

主持人：My pleasure. Cheers, lads.
